section_summary: This section documents Allied efforts to seize, examine, preserve, microfilm, transfer, or dispose of former Japanese diplomatic archives and property in Chile, Iraq, Egypt, Italy and the Vatican, Brazil, Sweden, the Netherlands, and other countries. Its largest items are a detailed intelligence report on the remnants of the Japanese Legation archives in Baghdad—including Iraqi firms trading with Japan, visa applicants, and Japanese personnel—and an English translation of former minister Yamagata’s Chile diary for August 1941–March 1942. Later documents address propaganda films, financial controls, reciprocal archival access, and the limited intelligence value of several recovered collections.

subfiles.title: Letter concerning Japanese archives and property in Chile
subfiles.about: British authorities consent to transferring Japanese archives to Washington and propose arrangements for Japanese property and funds in Chile.
subfiles.summary: Leche says British representatives must keep free access to archives sent to Washington, and recommends ending leases, selling or leasing government property, selling movables, treating seals as archives and reserving funds for protecting Japanese nationals.

subfiles.title: Departmental circulation and control sheets for Santiago despatch No. 13,246
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: The Department circulates the Santiago report on the ultimate disposal of Japanese official archives and property in Chile.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies despatch No. 13,246 of December 22, 1945, and distributes it to three intelligence agencies. The accompanying telegraph-control page records its receipt and filing under 894.414/12-2245.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on examination of Japanese archives in Mexico City
subfiles.from: Philip F. Cherp, Foreign Activity Correlation
subfiles.about: The Department declines to bring the Mexican archives to Washington and plans an on-site examination.
subfiles.summary: Cherp refers Mexico City despatch 27,641 and telegram 1329 for reply, asking it explain that qualified personnel will be sent from the U.S. to examine the archives.

subfiles.title: Vatican telegram No. 249 on Harada’s surrender of mission property
subfiles.about: Harada announces his readiness to surrender the Japanese mission’s property, funds, and archives and suspend relations with the Holy See.
subfiles.summary: Vatican telegram 249: Harada has Tokyo's instructions to deliver mission assets promptly to Allied representatives and then suspend relations; Gowen will cooperate with Montini and asks about a uniform press statement.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1001 transmitting the Baghdad archives report
subfiles.about: The Baghdad Legation transmits Lieutenant Colonel Welles’s report on the former Japanese Legation archives.
subfiles.summary: Moose endorses the Baghdad findings by Welles and Jeannette Pond despite Japanese diplomats' apparently thorough destruction of confidential records, and asks how to dispose of Japanese public property in Iraq.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding Welles’s report on the Japanese Legation records
subfiles.about: Welles forwards his report and recommends eventual destruction of records lacking further value.
subfiles.summary: Welles calls the surviving Japanese Legation records unsensational but a necessary intelligence clean-up, asks that Colonel Converse get the report and possible code pads, and advises keeping records only as long as the Allies need.

subfiles.title: Japanese Records in Iraq
subfiles.to: Strategic Services Unit and United States Legation, Baghdad
subfiles.about: A detailed report evaluates the surviving Japanese Legation records and extracts information on Iraqi trade, visa applicants, Japanese diplomats, businessmen, and students.
subfiles.summary: Welles reports that most confidential records had been burned before the Legation closed and that the remaining English-language files, books, equipment, and code pads held little intelligence value. The report reproduces a lengthy survey of Iraqi firms—many trading with Japan—and selected visa applications for travel to Japan. It also identifies Japanese Legation personnel, a convoy of Japanese businessmen departing Iraq, and Japanese students, concluding that further study would not be profitable.

subfiles.title: Visa Division search notes on the Baghdad enclosure
subfiles.about: Visa Division staff request a search and compare names found in the Baghdad report against visa records.
subfiles.summary: The notes ask for a thorough search relating to part of the enclosure to Baghdad despatch No. 1001. The heavily degraded handwriting records possible matches, including Luis Buchwald and several visa applicants, but much of the detail is illegible.

subfiles.title: Airgram A-27 requesting examination of the Japanese Legation safe
subfiles.about: The Department asks whether the unopened Japanese Legation safe has been forced and requests reports on its contents.
subfiles.summary: Airgram A-27 assumes the Japanese Legation safe in Welles's report has been opened and asks a full report by despatch and summary by airgram.

subfiles.title: Cairo telegram No. 2378 on transfer to Egyptian custody
subfiles.about: Tuck seeks instructions on a Soviet demand that Japanese property first pass formally to the Four Powers before Egyptian custody.
subfiles.summary: Cairo telegram 2378: the Swiss Minister may deliver property and archives to Egypt if Britain and the U.S. agree; Tuck considers the Soviet position legally sound and fears bypassing it would look like an Anglo-American front against the USSR.

subfiles.title: Telegram to Rome clarifying Tokyo’s instructions to Harada
subfiles.about: The Department states that Tokyo’s instruction to Harada should include surrendering keys to all mission archives.
subfiles.summary: Telegram to Rome: Tokyo considers its order to transfer all mission property, funds and archives explicit enough to cover keys; Rome should advise whether another directive is needed.

subfiles.title: Rome telegram No. 4210 on Four-Power custody of Japanese archives
subfiles.about: Rome reports Allied agreement in principle but inability to take physical possession until Harada surrenders the keys.
subfiles.summary: The Soviet and Chinese governments favor placing former Japanese diplomatic and consular property at the disposal of the Four Powers, with United States custody understood as temporary. Kirk says the representatives cannot take possession until Harada receives instructions to hand over the keys.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 2383 authorizing Egyptian custodianship
subfiles.about: The Department authorizes the Four Powers to entrust Japanese archives and property to the Egyptian Foreign Office if all representatives concur.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 2383: MacArthur's directive requires first transferring to the Four Powers; Egypt may then be custodian if it guarantees access and the four representatives agree.

subfiles.title: Record-copy replacement notice
subfiles.about: A white record copy is designated to replace an unreturned yellow action copy.
subfiles.summary: Records notice: a white copy replaces the missing action copy and should be returned for filing.

subfiles.title: Information copy of Cairo telegram No. 2378
subfiles.about: This duplicate records the dispute over whether Egyptian or Four-Power representatives should first receive Japanese archives and property.
subfiles.summary: Information copy of Cairo telegram 2378: Swiss propose direct Egyptian custody, the Soviets insist on formal Four-Power transfer; Tuck seeks instructions and warns against an Anglo-American bloc against Russia.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 13,242 transmitting Yamagata’s diary
subfiles.about: Bowers sends the first translated installment of former Japanese Minister Yamagata’s diary and comments on apparent leaks from the Chilean Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: Bowers highlights diary entries indicating that the German Embassy obtained an American note and details of his conversation with Rossetti. He attributes the possible disclosures to pro-Nazi Chilean officials Fernando Orrego Vicuña and Regulo Valenzuela Vera. He again recommends flying the small Japanese archival collection to Washington for examination.

subfiles.title: Some Facts in Former Japanese Minister Yamagata’s Diary
subfiles.from: Yamagata; translated by Su Shih Chen
subfiles.about: Diary extracts chronicle Japanese political, commercial, propaganda, and Axis diplomatic activity in Chile from August 1941 through March 1942.
subfiles.summary: Yamagata records efforts to expand Chilean-Japanese trade, release Legation funds, monitor Chilean politics, and maintain contact with officials and commercial intermediaries. After Pearl Harbor, the entries focus on protecting Japanese interests, coordinating with German, Italian, Spanish, and Argentine diplomats, assisting Japanese representatives stranded in South America, and countering Chilean alignment with the United States. The diary also notes propaganda work, military developments such as Singapore and Java, and negotiations over Irie, Yoshioka, shipping, and frozen funds.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3879 on Japanese archives in Brazil
subfiles.about: The Embassy transmits reports on Japanese archives at São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro and awaits disposal instructions.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 3879 encloses a Sao Paulo report on sealed cabinets and the Legal Attaché's Rio examination memorandum; archives and former Japanese property remain subject to Department instructions.

subfiles.title: São Paulo report on taking custody of Japanese Consulate records
subfiles.about: Welch reports sealing the Japanese Consulate’s cabinets, safe, and consular seal with his British colleague.
subfiles.summary: Sao Paulo: cabinets and a safe held mostly office supplies and almost no real archives; the Consulate General retains access to registration records at the Swedish Consulate.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the archives of the Japanese Embassy in Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.from: Office of the Legal Attaché, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: The memorandum describes the Allied takeover and examination of the former Japanese Embassy archives in Rio.
subfiles.summary: American, Chinese and British representatives took Rio Japanese Embassy archives from Sweden and searched cabinets, library, registration cards and films; no apparent intelligence value, significant records probably destroyed, several safes unopened, and the films were propaganda.

subfiles.title: Departmental distribution of despatch No. 3879
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: The Department distributes the Rio de Janeiro despatch on Japanese archives to intelligence agencies.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies despatch No. 3879 of December 29, 1945. Copies are supplied to military, naval, and federal investigative authorities.

subfiles.title: Vatican telegram No. 251 on suspension of relations and surrender of archives
subfiles.about: Gowen reports the suspension of Japanese relations with the Holy See and receipt of seven bundles of archives.
subfiles.summary: Vatican telegram 251: Harada told Montini relations were suspended as of December 31, 1945; Montini delivered seven bundles of documents to Allied representatives for joint intelligence examination; Gowen asks about furniture, effects and about $22,000 in Vatican Bank funds.

subfiles.title: Information copy of Vatican telegram No. 251
subfiles.about: This duplicate reports receipt of the Japanese Vatican archives and proposals for handling mission property and funds.
subfiles.summary: The information copy repeats that seven bundles were delivered following the suspension of Japanese-Holy See relations. It also repeats the plan for Allied examination and the practical proposal to claim, but temporarily leave in place, assets needed by the Japanese group.

subfiles.title: Correction changing Vatican telegram 251 to telegram 1
subfiles.about: The sender corrects the serial number of the January 1 telegram from 251 to 1.
subfiles.summary: Correction: Vatican telegram issued as No. 251 should read No. 1, dated January 1, 3 p.m.

subfiles.title: Second correction of the Vatican telegram serial number
subfiles.about: A second correction copy confirms that telegram 251 should be numbered 1.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate correction of the Vatican telegram's serial number; filed under Japanese relations with the Holy See.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3904 on shipment of Japanese archival material
subfiles.about: The Embassy reports the planned shipment to Washington of films and other items from the former Japanese Embassy.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 3904 supplements No. 3879, enclosing a January 2 Legal Attaché memorandum on material selected from the Rio Japanese Embassy for shipment to Washington.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on shipping Japanese films, passports, and publications
subfiles.about: Clegg reports arrangements to send Japanese propaganda films, unused passports, books, and pamphlets to Washington.
subfiles.summary: Shipment of about fifty-one cans of 35mm film, fifty unused Japanese passports and publications on Japanese culture and industry; British and Chinese representatives approved and keep access in Washington.

subfiles.title: Departmental distribution of despatch No. 3904
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: The Department circulates the Rio report on shipment of Japanese archival items.
subfiles.summary: Distribution sheet sending despatch 3904 of January 4, 1946 to military, naval and federal investigative agencies.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 22 requesting Moscow’s current position
subfiles.about: The Department asks whether the Moscow Embassy’s position on Japanese archives has changed.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 22 asks Moscow to confirm the Embassy's current position, citing Moscow telegram 4030 of December 3 and recent developments.

subfiles.title: Circular telegram on Japanese mission funds in the American republics
subfiles.from: James F. Byrnes, Department of State
subfiles.to: All American diplomatic missions in the other American republics
subfiles.about: The Department orders Japanese mission funds held in trust for the Four Powers while permitting accountable routine expenditures by protecting powers.
subfiles.summary: Secret circular: all cash and liquid resources of Japanese missions in the American republics go under Allied control for the U.S., Soviets, Britain and China; protecting powers may continue routine functions under access and accounting arrangements; await a fuller airgram.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on missing Japanese financial documents
subfiles.to: Chief, Foreign Press Section, Military Intelligence Service
subfiles.about: PACMIRS reports that Japanese financial documents concerning Germany cannot be located.
subfiles.summary: War Department: searches at the Washington Document Center and Camp Ritchie found no record of receiving the missing Japanese financial documents; PACMIRS will keep watching and report.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to J. E. MacDonald on the missing financial documents
subfiles.about: Lyon reports the War Department’s unsuccessful search for Japanese financial documents.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum to J. E. MacDonald traces the inquiry to an October 1945 request on documents in USFET serial CD-125; neither Washington nor Camp Ritchie received them, and the War Department will watch and advise State.

subfiles.title: Corrected Vatican telegram No. 2 on preliminary examination
subfiles.about: Allied intelligence officers find little immediate military value in the Vatican archives but propose microfilming Japanese-language records.
subfiles.summary: Corrected Vatican telegram 2: American, British and French G-2 officers examined the documents January 3, with British and Chinese ministers concurring; Gowen asks final disposition after proposed microfilming for the War Department.

subfiles.title: Uncorrected action copy of Vatican telegram No. 2
subfiles.about: This incomplete copy reports the preliminary Allied review of the Japanese Vatican archives.
subfiles.summary: Uncorrected action copy of Vatican telegram 2, with an omission in the intelligence-value sentence; it records the microfilming proposal and asks what to do with the originals.

subfiles.title: Circular airgram on control and accounting of Japanese mission assets
subfiles.from: James F. Byrnes, Department of State
subfiles.to: All American diplomatic missions in the other American republics
subfiles.about: The Department issues detailed procedures for controlling Japanese mission funds and sale proceeds.
subfiles.summary: Secret circular airgram: protecting powers' public and private liquid assets go into accountable trust arrangements for the Four Powers; routine relief, expenses, moving and storage may be paid, extraordinary costs like repatriation need authorization; missions report balances and quarterly accounts.

subfiles.title: Telegram to SCAP requesting instructions to surrender archive keys
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo, for Acheson
subfiles.about: The Department asks Tokyo to ensure that Harada receives explicit orders to surrender the keys to the former Japanese Embassy archives in Italy.
subfiles.summary: Telegram to SCAP: Rome reports possession can't be obtained while Harada keeps the archive keys; SCAP is asked to advise when the instructions are issued.

subfiles.title: Moscow telegram No. 87 on disposition of Japanese archives
subfiles.about: The Moscow Embassy confirms that its position on Japanese archives remains unchanged.
subfiles.summary: The brief reply answers Department telegram No. 22. It states without elaboration that the Embassy’s prior position still stands.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 13 requesting the status of Japanese archives in Siam
subfiles.about: The Department asks for a report on Japanese diplomatic and consular archives and property in Siam.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 13 explains the U.S. sought worldwide Four-Power custody of Japanese archives under MacArthur's directive and asks Bangkok to report the situation in Siam.

subfiles.title: Stockholm telegram No. 73 on Japanese intelligence personnel
subfiles.about: Commander Taylor recommends interrogating Japanese intelligence officers interned in Sweden despite the limited value of the Legation archives.
subfiles.summary: Stockholm telegram 73: Taylor judges the archives of little intelligence value, proposes returning via Madrid to brief officials, and urges sending interrogators to question General Onodera, former naval attaché Abe and assistants, allowing cross-checking with Legation files.

subfiles.title: Cairo telegram No. 54 on agreed Egyptian custodianship
subfiles.about: The Four-Power representatives agree that Switzerland will transfer Japanese property to them and that they will entrust it to Egyptian custody.
subfiles.summary: Cairo telegram 54: a meeting with the Egyptian under secretary and Swiss Minister produced a compromise; the Soviet agreed in principle but wants a short delay for Moscow's authorization.

subfiles.title: Record-copy replacement notice
subfiles.about: A white copy is designated as the record copy because the original yellow action copy was not returned.
subfiles.summary: The notice documents a records-control substitution. It instructs staff to return the attached copy for filing.

subfiles.title: Vatican telegram on cooperation concerning Japanese personnel
subfiles.about: The badly degraded telegram reports cooperation concerning Japanese personnel, apparently in connection with repatriation.
subfiles.summary: Fragmentary Vatican telegram stating Gowen is cooperating and mentioning repatriating Japanese personnel; the requested action can't be reconstructed.

subfiles.title: The Hague telegram No. 46 on reciprocal access to Japanese archives
subfiles.doc_type: incoming secret telegram with duplicate copy
subfiles.about: The Netherlands offers Allied access to Japanese archives under its control while requesting reciprocal access to collections held by the Four Powers.
subfiles.summary: The Dutch Foreign Office is investigating whether Japanese archives remain in the Netherlands or its overseas territories. Britain considers the reciprocity request reasonable, and Hornbeck recommends coordinating a mutually satisfactory reply after instructions arrive. Soviet and Chinese views were not yet known.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 82 replying to the Dutch reciprocity proposal
subfiles.about: The Department accepts reciprocal access in principle, subject to limits and Allied concurrence.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 82 on the Dutch reciprocity proposal: Dutch access would cover only archives seized in each government's own territory, no reply until Soviet and Chinese concurrence and confirmation that Japanese archives exist.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 546 transmitting Dutch correspondence on Japanese archives
subfiles.about: Hornbeck forwards correspondence between the British Ambassador and the Netherlands Foreign Ministry about Japanese archives.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 546, answering the Department's January 11 telegram, encloses the British proposal for coordinated action and the Dutch offer of access conditioned on reciprocity.

subfiles.title: British Ambassador’s letter proposing a coordinated reply
subfiles.about: Bland asks Hornbeck to join in a coordinated response to the Dutch request for reciprocal archival access.
subfiles.summary: British Ambassador encloses the Dutch Foreign Ministry's reply to his request for examination rights, finds reciprocity reasonable, and proposes the Allied representatives agree on a common answer.

subfiles.title: Netherlands Foreign Ministry note on Japanese diplomatic and consular archives
subfiles.from: Secretary-General, Netherlands Ministry of Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: The Netherlands agrees to share access to Japanese archives in Dutch territory and requests equivalent access to Allied-held archives concerning Dutch interests.
subfiles.summary: Netherlands Foreign Ministry is investigating whether Japanese records remain in the Netherlands or overseas, offers Britain, the U.S., China and the Soviets access, and asks reciprocal examination rights for Dutch representatives.
